title: Tutorial 01 – Crystal Structure and Energy Bands
text:
1 Learning objectives

Describe the crystal structure of silicon.
Explain how energy bands arise in a solid.
Distinguish metals, semiconductors, and insulators by their band gap.

title: Tutorial 01 – Crystal Structure and Energy Bands
text:
2 From atoms to energy bands
When many atoms come together in a lattice, their discrete energy levels broaden into bands. The gap between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band is the band gap, \(E_g\).

Animation: the atomic levels of N atoms split and merge into the valence and conduction bands.



Material
Band gap \(E_g\) at 300 K




Silicon (Si)
1.12 eV


Germanium (Ge)
0.66 eV


Gallium arsenide (GaAs)
1.42 eV

title: Tutorial 01 – Crystal Structure and Energy Bands
text:
3 Intrinsic carrier concentration
In an intrinsic semiconductor, electrons and holes are generated in pairs:
\[
n_i = \sqrt{N_c N_v}\, e^{-E_g / 2kT}
\]



Approximate \(n_i\) of silicon versus temperature (constant \(E_g = 1.12\) eV).

title: Tutorial 01 – Crystal Structure and Energy Bands
text:
4 Summary

Bands form because atomic levels split when atoms are brought together.
The band gap \(E_g\) decides whether a solid behaves as a metal, semiconductor, or insulator.
\(n_i\) grows exponentially with temperature.







NoteExercise



Why does \(n_i\) rise so quickly with temperature?

text:
2 Problem Set

2.1 Problem 1 (Lecture Problem 5)
Two cables exert forces \(F_B = 600\text{ lb}\) and \(F_C = 750\text{ lb}\) on the hook at \(A(0, 0, 4\text{ ft})\), anchored at \(B(3\text{ ft}, -3\text{ ft}, 2.5\text{ ft})\) and \(C(2\text{ ft}, 4\text{ ft}, 0\text{ ft})\). Determine the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of the resultant force acting at \(A\).





























































































































































































































































































































TipSolution Key — Problem 1 (Lecture Problem 5)






\(\mathbf{r}_{AB} = 3\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 1.5\mathbf{k}\text{ ft}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{AB}| = 4.5\text{ ft} \implies \mathbf{F}_B = 600\left(\frac{3\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 1.5\mathbf{k}}{4.5}\right) = \{400\mathbf{i} - 400\mathbf{j} - 200\mathbf{k}\}\text{ lb}\)
\(\mathbf{r}_{AC} = 2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}\text{ ft}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{AC}| = 6\text{ ft} \implies \mathbf{F}_C = 750\left(\frac{2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}}{6}\right) = \{250\mathbf{i} + 500\mathbf{j} - 500\mathbf{k}\}\text{ lb}\)
\(\mathbf{F}_R = \mathbf{F}_B + \mathbf{F}_C = \{650\mathbf{i} + 100\mathbf{j} - 700\mathbf{k}\}\text{ lb}\)
\(F_R = \sqrt{650^2 + 100^2 + (-700)^2} = 960.5\text{ lb}\)
\(\alpha = 47.4^\circ, \quad \beta = 84.0^\circ, \quad \gamma = 136.8^\circ\)







2.2 Problem 2 (Lecture Problem 6)
Two cables attached to ring \(A(0, -2\text{ m}, 4\text{ m})\) carry tensions of \(600\text{ N}\) (directed toward \(B(0, 0, 0)\)) and \(500\text{ N}\) (directed toward \(C\), located at \(x_C = 4\text{ m}\) and \(8\text{ m}\) in the \(+y\) direction from \(A\), i.e., \(C(4\text{ m}, 6\text{ m}, 0)\)). Determine the magnitude and the coordinate direction angles of the resultant force.





















































































































































































































































































TipSolution Key — Problem 2 (Lecture Problem 6)






\(\mathbf{r}_{AB} = 0\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}\text{ m}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{AB}| = \sqrt{20} = 4.472\text{ m} \implies \mathbf{F}_{AB} = \{268.33\mathbf{j} - 536.66\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(\mathbf{r}_{AC} = 4\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}\text{ m}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{AC}| = \sqrt{96} = 9.798\text{ m} \implies \mathbf{F}_{AC} = \{204.12\mathbf{i} + 408.25\mathbf{j} - 204.12\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(\mathbf{F}_R = \{204.12\mathbf{i} + 676.58\mathbf{j} - 740.78\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(F_R = 1024\text{ N}, \quad \alpha = 78.5^\circ, \quad \beta = 48.6^\circ, \quad \gamma = 136.3^\circ\)







2.3 Problem 3 (Lecture Problem 7)
A rifle at \(A\) (\(z_A = 80\text{ m}\)) is fired at a target at \(B\) across a range with horizontal offsets \(\Delta x = 160\text{ m}\), \(\Delta y = 210\text{ m}\), and \(\Delta z = -80\text{ m}\). If the speed of the bullet is \(1800\text{ m/s}\), determine the rectangular form of the velocity vector \(\mathbf{v}\).






































































































































































































TipSolution Key — Problem 3 (Lecture Problem 7)






\(\mathbf{r}_{AB} = 160\mathbf{i} + 210\mathbf{j} - 80\mathbf{k}\text{ m} \quad (\text{or } -160\mathbf{i} + 210\mathbf{j} - 80\mathbf{k}\text{ m depending on origin choice})\)
\(|\mathbf{r}_{AB}| = \sqrt{160^2 + 210^2 + (-80)^2} = \sqrt{76100} = 275.86\text{ m}\)
\(\mathbf{v} = 1800\frac{\mathbf{r}_{AB}}{|\mathbf{r}_{AB}|} = \{1044\mathbf{i} + 1370\mathbf{j} - 522\mathbf{k}\}\text{ m/s}\)







2.4 Problem 4 (Lecture Problem 8)
The slider travels along the guide rod \(AB\) from \(A(10\text{ m}, -8\text{ m}, 0)\) to \(B(0, 16\text{ m}, 12\text{ m})\) with a velocity \(v = 6\text{ m/s}\). Determine the rectangular representations of (a) the unit vector directed from \(A\) toward \(B\); and (b) the velocity vector \(\mathbf{v}\).


































































































































































































































TipSolution Key — Problem 4 (Lecture Problem 8)






\(\mathbf{r}_{AB} = (0 - 10)\mathbf{i} + (16 - (-8))\mathbf{j} + (12 - 0)\mathbf{k} = -10\mathbf{i} + 24\mathbf{j} + 12\mathbf{k}\text{ m}\)
\(|\mathbf{r}_{AB}| = \sqrt{(-10)^2 + 24^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{820} = 28.636\text{ m}\)
(a) \(\mathbf{u}_{AB} = -0.349\mathbf{i} + 0.838\mathbf{j} + 0.419\mathbf{k}\)
(b) \(\mathbf{v} = 6\mathbf{u}_{AB} = \{-2.10\mathbf{i} + 5.03\mathbf{j} + 2.51\mathbf{k}\}\text{ m/s}\)







2.5 Problem 5 (Lecture Problem 9)
Two cables attached to the top of post \(C(0, 0, 4\text{ ft})\) exert forces \(F_1 = 100\text{ lb}\) (toward \(A\), located in the \(xy\)-plane at radius \(3\text{ ft}\) and angle \(40^\circ\) from the \(+y\) axis toward the \(-x\) axis) and \(F_2 = 81\text{ lb}\) (toward \(B(4\text{ ft}, -7\text{ ft}, 0)\)). Determine the magnitude and the coordinate direction angles of the resultant force.







































































































































































































































































































































TipSolution Key — Problem 5 (Lecture Problem 9)






\(A(-3\sin 40^\circ, 3\cos 40^\circ, 0) = (-1.928\text{ ft}, 2.298\text{ ft}, 0)\)
\(\mathbf{r}_{CA} = -1.928\mathbf{i} + 2.298\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}\text{ ft}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{CA}| = 5\text{ ft} \implies \mathbf{F}_1 = \{-38.57\mathbf{i} + 45.96\mathbf{j} - 80.00\mathbf{k}\}\text{ lb}\)
\(\mathbf{r}_{CB} = 4\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}\text{ ft}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{CB}| = 9\text{ ft} \implies \mathbf{F}_2 = \{36.00\mathbf{i} - 63.00\mathbf{j} - 36.00\mathbf{k}\}\text{ lb}\)
\(\mathbf{F}_R = \{-2.57\mathbf{i} - 17.04\mathbf{j} - 116.00\mathbf{k}\}\text{ lb}\)
\(F_R = 117.3\text{ lb}, \quad \alpha = 91.3^\circ, \quad \beta = 98.4^\circ, \quad \gamma = 171.6^\circ\)







2.6 Problem 6 (Lecture Problem 10)
The tower of height \(24\text{ m}\) at \(D(0, 0, 24\text{ m})\) is held in place by three cables anchored at \(A(x, y, 0)\), \(B(-6\text{ m}, 4\text{ m}, 0)\), and \(C(16\text{ m}, -18\text{ m}, 0)\) with forces \(F_{DA} = 400\text{ N}\), \(F_{DB} = 800\text{ N}\), and \(F_{DC} = 600\text{ N}\). Taking \(x = 20\text{ m}\) and \(y = 15\text{ m}\), determine the magnitude and coordinate direction angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) of the resultant force.








































































































































































































































































































































































TipSolution Key — Problem 6 (Lecture Problem 10)






\(\mathbf{r}_{DA} = 20\mathbf{i} + 15\mathbf{j} - 24\mathbf{k}\text{ m}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{DA}| = \sqrt{1201} = 34.655\text{ m} \implies \mathbf{F}_{DA} = \{230.85\mathbf{i} + 173.13\mathbf{j} - 277.01\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(\mathbf{r}_{DB} = -6\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 24\mathbf{k}\text{ m}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{DB}| = \sqrt{628} = 25.060\text{ m} \implies \mathbf{F}_{DB} = \{-191.54\mathbf{i} + 127.69\mathbf{j} - 766.16\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(\mathbf{r}_{DC} = 16\mathbf{i} - 18\mathbf{j} - 24\mathbf{k}\text{ m}, \quad |\mathbf{r}_{DC}| = 34\text{ m} \implies \mathbf{F}_{DC} = \{282.35\mathbf{i} - 317.65\mathbf{j} - 423.53\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(\mathbf{F}_R = \{321.66\mathbf{i} - 16.82\mathbf{j} - 1466.70\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\)
\(F_R = 1502\text{ N} \approx 1.50\text{ kN}, \quad \alpha = 77.6^\circ, \quad \beta = 90.6^\circ, \quad \gamma = 167.6^\circ\)

title: Tutorial 01 – Fundamental Antenna Parameters
text:
2 Radiation pattern, directivity, and gain
Directivity is the ratio of radiation intensity in a given direction to the average radiation intensity:
\[
D(\theta,\phi) = \frac{4\pi\, U(\theta,\phi)}{P_{\text{rad}}}
\]
Gain includes losses through the radiation efficiency \(e_r\):
\[
G = e_r \, D
\]



Normalized elevation pattern of a half-wave dipole.

title: Tutorial 01 – Fundamental Antenna Parameters

\[
P_r = P_t \, G_t \, G_r \left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi R}\right)^2
\]






NoteExercise

title: Tutorial 01: 3D Cartesian Vectors & Position Vectors
text:
Engineering mechanics relies on four basic quantities:

Length: Used to locate the position of a point in space and describe the size of a physical system; once a standard unit of length is defined, distances and geometric properties of a body are expressed as multiples of this unit.
Time: Conceived as a succession of events; while the principles of statics are time-independent, time plays an important role in dynamics.
Mass: A measure of a quantity of matter used to compare the action of one body with another; it manifests as gravitational attraction between two bodies and measures the resistance of matter to a change in velocity.
Force: Considered as a “push” or “pull” exerted by one body on another, occurring either through direct contact (such as pushing on a wall) or through a distance when physically separated (such as gravitational, electrical, and magnetic forces). A force is completely characterized by its magnitude, direction, and point of application.

title: Tutorial 01: 3D Cartesian Vectors & Position Vectors
text:
2 From 2D to 3D Rectangular Components

2.1 2D Review vs. 3D Extension
In two dimensions, a vector \(\mathbf{A}\) making an angle \(\theta\) with the positive \(x\)-axis is resolved into rectangular components using simple right-triangle trigonometry:
\[A_x = A \cos\theta, \quad A_y = A \sin\theta\]
\[\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{} = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}, \quad \angle\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right)\]
In three dimensions, vector algebra operations are greatly simplified by expressing vectors in Cartesian vector form.


2.2 Right-Handed Coordinate System
We use a right-handed coordinate system where the positive \(z\)-axis is directed upward (the zenith direction) to measure height or altitude, while the \(x\) and \(y\) axes lie in the horizontal plane. A rectangular coordinate system is right-handed if the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of the positive \(z\)-axis when the right-hand fingers are curled about this axis from the positive \(x\)-axis toward the positive \(y\)-axis.






WarningWatch Your Axis Orientation!



Swapping the positive \(x\) and \(y\) axes so that curling your fingers from \(+x\) to \(+y\) points your thumb downward creates a left-handed coordinate system, which is wrong for our vector formulations. Always verify your axes using the right-hand rule before reading coordinates.





2.3 Rectangular & Cartesian Vector Representation
When a vector \(\mathbf{A}\) is directed within an octant of the \(x, y, z\) frame, two successive applications of the parallelogram law resolve the vector first into \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}' + \mathbf{A}_z\) (where \(\mathbf{A}'\) is the projection in the \(xy\)-plane) and then \(\mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A}_x + \mathbf{A}_y\), yielding the vector sum:
\[\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}_x + \mathbf{A}_y + \mathbf{A}_z\]






ImportantTA Note: Separate Magnitude and Direction



Writing \(A = A_x + A_y + A_z\) as a scalar sum is not accurate because each component has both a magnitude and a distinct axis direction. Using the Cartesian unit vectors \(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}\) along the positive \(x, y, z\) axes separates the scalar magnitude (\(A_x, A_y, A_z\)) from the direction (\(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}\)):
\[\mathbf{A} = A_x\mathbf{i} + A_y\mathbf{j} + A_z\mathbf{k}\]




2.4 Magnitude of a Cartesian Vector
From the two right triangles formed by the 3D parallelepiped, \(A = \sqrt{A'^2 + A_z^2}\) and \(A' = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}\). Combining these equations to eliminate \(A'\) gives the magnitude of \(\mathbf{A}\) as the positive square root of the sum of the squares of its components:
\[\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{} = A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}\]

title: Tutorial 01: 3D Cartesian Vectors & Position Vectors
text:
3 Direction Cosines & Unit Vectors

3.1 Coordinate Direction Angles (\(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\))
The direction of a Cartesian vector \(\mathbf{A}\) is defined by the coordinate direction angles \(\alpha\) (alpha), \(\beta\) (beta), and \(\gamma\) (gamma)—also abbreviated as \(\theta_x = \alpha\), \(\theta_y = \beta\), and \(\theta_z = \gamma\)—measured between the tail of \(\mathbf{A}\) and the positive \(x, y, z\) axes located at the tail of \(\mathbf{A}\). Regardless of where \(\mathbf{A}\) is directed, each angle lies between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\).
Projecting \(\mathbf{A}\) onto the \(x, y, z\) axes forms three right triangles that define the direction cosines of \(\mathbf{A}\):
\[\cos\alpha = \frac{A_x}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}, \quad \cos\beta = \frac{A_y}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}, \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{A_z}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\]
Note also that if the angle \(\gamma\) with the \(z\)-axis is given, the intermediate projection onto the \(xy\)-plane has magnitude \(A' = A\sin\gamma\).


3.2 Unit Vector (\(\mathbf{u}_A\)) and Direction Cosine Identity
Dividing \(\mathbf{A}\) by its magnitude \(\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}\) produces a dimensionless unit vector \(\mathbf{u}_A\) of magnitude \(1\) pointing in the direction of \(\mathbf{A}\):
\[\mathbf{u}_A = \frac{\mathbf{A}}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}} = \frac{A_x}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\mathbf{i} + \frac{A_y}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\mathbf{j} + \frac{A_z}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\mathbf{k} = \cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + \cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + \cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}\]
Because the magnitude of \(\mathbf{u}_A\) is equal to \(1\), the sum of the squares of the direction cosines satisfies the fundamental identity:
\[\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\]
If any two of the coordinate direction angles are known, the third angle can be found using this equation. Furthermore, if the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of \(\mathbf{A}\) are known, \(\mathbf{A}\) is expressed in Cartesian vector form as:
\[\mathbf{A} = \vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}\cdot\mathbf{u}_A = A\cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + A\cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + A\cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}\]

title: Tutorial 01: 3D Cartesian Vectors & Position Vectors
section: 4 Position Vectors & Force Along a Line
text:
4 Position Vectors & Force Along a Line
A position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) is a fixed vector that locates a point in space relative to another point:

From the Origin (\(O\) to \(P\)): If \(\mathbf{r}\) extends from the origin of coordinates \(O(0,0,0)\) to a point \(P(x, y, z)\), then: \[\mathbf{r} = P - O = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + z\mathbf{k}\] For example, starting at \(O\), measuring \(x_A = +4\text{ m}\), \(y_A = +2\text{ m}\), and \(z_A = -6\text{ m}\) locates \(A(4\text{ m}, 2\text{ m}, -6\text{ m})\), while \(B(6\text{ m}, -1\text{ m}, 4\text{ m})\) is located at \(x_B = +6\text{ m}\), \(y_B = -1\text{ m}\), and \(z_B = +4\text{ m}\).
Between Two Points (\(A\) to \(B\)): For a position vector directed from an initial point \(A(x_A, y_A, z_A)\) to a terminal point \(B(x_B, y_B, z_B)\) (or from \(P\) to \(Q\)), head-to-tail triangle addition requires \(\mathbf{r}_A + \mathbf{r}_{AB} = \mathbf{r}_B\), giving the difference between the two points (“destination minus origin”): \[\mathbf{r}_{AB} = \mathbf{r}_B - \mathbf{r}_A = (x_B - x_A)\mathbf{i} + (y_B - y_A)\mathbf{j} + (z_B - z_A)\mathbf{k}\]

To express a force \(\mathbf{F}\) of known magnitude \(F\) directed along a cable or line from \(A\) to \(B\), multiply the scalar magnitude \(F\) by the unit vector \(\mathbf{u}_{AB} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_{AB}}{\vert{}\mathbf{r}_{AB}\vert{}}\).

title: Tutorial 01: 3D Cartesian Vectors & Position Vectors
text:
5 Worked Lecture Examples

5.1 Example 1: Force Directed Along a Cable
Problem: A cable attached to an eyebolt at \(A(4\text{ m}, 0, 3\text{ m})\) is pulled toward point \(B(0, 6\text{ m}, 0)\) with a force \(\mathbf{F}\) of magnitude \(500\text{ N}\). Determine the rectangular representation of this force.









































































































































































































































Solution:

Write the position vector \(\vec{AB}\) from \(A\) to \(B\) in rectangular form: Avoid common errors (choosing the wrong signs or mixing up scalar components) by sketching the parallelepiped from \(A\) to \(B\): \[\vec{AB} = -4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}\text{ m}\]
Evaluate the unit vector \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} = \mathbf{u}_{AB}\) from \(A\) toward \(B\): \[\mathbf{u}_{AB} = \boldsymbol{\lambda} = \frac{\vec{AB}}{\vert{}\vec{AB}\vert{}} = \frac{-4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{(-4)^2 + 6^2 + (-3)^2}} = -0.5122\mathbf{i} + 0.7682\mathbf{j} - 0.3841\mathbf{k}\]
Multiply by the magnitude of the force (\(F = 500\text{ N}\)): \[\mathbf{F} = F\boldsymbol{\lambda} = 500(-0.5122\mathbf{i} + 0.7682\mathbf{j} - 0.3841\mathbf{k}) = \{-256\mathbf{i} + 384\mathbf{j} - 192\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\]




5.2 Example 2: Force from Coordinate Direction Angles
Problem: Express the force \(F = 200\text{ N}\) acting in the first octant with \(\beta = 60^\circ\) and \(\gamma = 45^\circ\) as a Cartesian vector.








































































































































































































Solution:

Find the unknown coordinate direction angle \(\alpha\): Using the direction cosine identity: \[\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \implies \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2 45^\circ = 1\]
(Note: The lecture slide contains a typographical error printing \(\cos^2 0^\circ\) and \((0)^2\) in the intermediate substitution line instead of \(\cos^2 60^\circ = (0.5)^2\), though its final root \(\pm 0.5\) is based on \(\beta = 60^\circ\).) \[\cos\alpha = \sqrt{1 - (0.5)^2 - (0.707)^2} = \pm 0.5 \implies \alpha = \cos^{-1}(0.5) = 60^\circ \text{ or } \cos^{-1}(-0.5) = 120^\circ\]
Because the force vector points in the positive \(x\) direction, we select \(\alpha = 60^\circ\).
Express \(\mathbf{F}\) in Cartesian vector form: \[\mathbf{F} = F\cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + F\cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + F\cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}\]
\[\mathbf{F} = (200\cos 60^\circ\text{ N})\mathbf{i} + (200\cos 60^\circ\text{ N})\mathbf{j} + (200\cos 45^\circ\text{ N})\mathbf{k} = \{100.0\mathbf{i} + 100.0\mathbf{j} + 141.4\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\]




5.3 Example 3: Double-Projection Resolution (\(A_{xy}\) Method)
Problem: For the position vector \(\mathbf{A}\) of magnitude \(A = 12\text{ m}\) making an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the positive \(z\)-axis and whose projection in the \(xy\)-plane makes an angle of \(40^\circ\) with the positive \(x\)-axis toward the positive \(y\)-axis, determine (1) the rectangular representation of \(\mathbf{A}\) and (2) the angles between \(\mathbf{A}\) and each of the positive coordinate axes.












































































































































































































Solution:

Resolve \(\mathbf{A}\) into vertical (\(A_z\)) and horizontal (\(A_{xy}\)) components, then resolve \(A_{xy}\) into \(A_x\) and \(A_y\): \[A_z = A\cos 30^\circ = 12\cos 30^\circ = 10.392\text{ m}\]
\[A_{xy} = A\sin 30^\circ = 12\sin 30^\circ = 6\text{ m}\]
\[A_x = A_{xy}\cos 40^\circ = 6\cos 40^\circ = 4.596\text{ m}\]
\[A_y = A_{xy}\sin 40^\circ = 6\sin 40^\circ = 3.857\text{ m}\]
\[\mathbf{A} = A_x\mathbf{i} + A_y\mathbf{j} + A_z\mathbf{k} = \{4.60\mathbf{i} + 3.86\mathbf{j} + 10.39\mathbf{k}\}\text{ m}\]
Calculate the coordinate direction angles (\(\theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z\)): \[\theta_x = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_x}{A}\right) = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4.596}{12}\right) = 67.5^\circ\]
\[\theta_y = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_y}{A}\right) = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3.857}{12}\right) = 71.3^\circ\]
\[\theta_z = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_z}{A}\right) = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{10.392}{12}\right) = 30.0^\circ\]




5.4 Example 4: Obtuse Coordinate Direction Angles
Problem: Express the force \(F = 500\text{ N}\) (directed in the \(+x, -y, -z\) octant, making \(45^\circ\) with the negative \(y\)-axis and \(60^\circ\) with the negative \(z\)-axis) as a Cartesian vector.






























































































































































































































Solution:

Determine the coordinate direction angles from the positive axes: Since the vector makes \(45^\circ\) with \(-y\) and \(60^\circ\) with \(-z\), the supplementary angles measured from the positive \(y\) and \(z\) axes are \(\beta = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ\) and \(\gamma = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). \[\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2 135^\circ + \cos^2 120^\circ = 1 \implies \alpha = 60^\circ\]
Write the Cartesian vector: \[\mathbf{F} = F\mathbf{u}_F = (500\text{ N})(0.5\mathbf{i} - 0.7071\mathbf{j} - 0.5\mathbf{k}) = \{250\mathbf{i} - 354\mathbf{j} - 250\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\]

title: Tutorial 01: 3D Cartesian Vectors & Position Vectors
text:
6 Guided Tutorial Practice Problems (Problems 1–4)

6.1 Problem 1
Statement: Obtain the rectangular representation of the force \(\mathbf{P}\), given that its magnitude is \(30\text{ N}\), it is inclined at \(50^\circ\) above its projection in the \(xy\)-plane, and its \(xy\)-plane projection makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the \(+y\) axis toward the \(-x\) axis.































































































































































































Solution:

Project \(\mathbf{P}\) onto the \(z\)-axis and the \(xy\)-plane: \[P_z = 30\sin 50^\circ = 22.98\text{ N} \approx 23\text{ N}\]
\[P_{xy} = 30\cos 50^\circ = 19.28\text{ N}\]
Resolve \(P_{xy}\) along the \(-x\) and \(+y\) axes: \[P_x = -P_{xy}\sin 30^\circ = -19.28(0.5) = -9.64\text{ N}\] \[P_y = P_{xy}\cos 30^\circ = 19.28(0.8660) = 16.70\text{ N}\] \[\mathbf{P} = \{-9.64\mathbf{i} + 16.70\mathbf{j} + 22.98\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}\]







NoteTA Caution on Slide Annotations



The handwritten annotation on the lecture slide lists \(P_x = -15\), \(P_y = 15\sqrt{3}\), and \(P_z = 23\). Notice that \(-15 = -30\sin 30^\circ\) and \(15\sqrt{3} = 30\cos 30^\circ\), which resolves the full \(30\text{ N}\) magnitude directly in the \(xy\)-plane without first multiplying by \(\cos 50^\circ\)! Always project onto the \(xy\)-plane (\(P_{xy} = P\cos 50^\circ\)) before resolving into \(x\) and \(y\) components.





6.2 Problem 2
Statement: The force \(\mathbf{F}\) acts on the bracket within the octant shown. If \(F = 400\text{ N}\), \(\beta = 60^\circ\), and \(\gamma = 45^\circ\), determine the \(x, y, z\) components of \(\mathbf{F}\).




























































































































































































































Solution:

Using \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\): \[\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2 45^\circ = 1 \implies \cos\alpha = \pm 0.5\]
Since \(\mathbf{F}\) is directed into the \(-x, +y, +z\) octant (\(\alpha = 120^\circ\)), \(\cos\alpha = -0.5\) (magnitude \(\vert{}F_x\vert{} = 200\text{ N}\)): \[F_x = -400(0.5) = -200\text{ N} \quad (\text{magnitude } 200\text{ N})\] \[F_y = 400\cos 60^\circ = 200\text{ N}\] \[F_z = 400\cos 45^\circ = 282.843\text{ N}\]




6.3 Problem 3
Statement: Determine the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of \(\mathbf{F}_2\) so that the resultant of the two forces (\(\mathbf{F}_1 = 180\text{ N}\) and \(\mathbf{F}_2\)) acts along the positive \(x\)-axis and has a magnitude of \(500\text{ N}\).
















































































































































































































































Solution:

Resolve \(\mathbf{F}_1 = 180\text{ N}\) into components: \(\mathbf{F}_1\) is inclined \(15^\circ\) below the \(xy\)-plane along a projection line \(60^\circ\) from the \(+y\) axis toward the \(+x\) axis: \[F_{1x} = (180\cos 15^\circ)\sin 60^\circ = 150.57\text{ N}\] \[F_{1y} = (180\cos 15^\circ)\cos 60^\circ = 86.93\text{ N}\] \[F_{1z} = -180\sin 15^\circ = -46.59\text{ N}\]
Apply \(\mathbf{F}_R = \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 = 500\mathbf{i}\text{ N}\): \[F_{2x} = 500 - 150.57 = 349.43\text{ N}\] \[F_{2y} = 0 - 86.93 = -86.93\text{ N}\] \[F_{2z} = 0 - (-46.59) = 46.59\text{ N}\]
Compute the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of \(\mathbf{F}_2\): \[F_2 = \sqrt{(349.43)^2 + (-86.93)^2 + (46.59)^2} = 363.1\text{ N}\] \[\alpha_2 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{349.43}{363.1}\right) = 15.8^\circ, \quad \beta_2 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-86.93}{363.1}\right) = 103.9^\circ, \quad \gamma_2 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{46.59}{363.1}\right) = 82.6^\circ\]




6.4 Problem 4
Statement: The pole is subjected to the force \(\mathbf{F}\) which has components \(F_x = 1.5\text{ kN}\) and \(F_z = 1.25\text{ kN}\). If \(\beta = 75^\circ\), determine the magnitudes of \(\mathbf{F}\) and \(F_y\).













































































































































































































































Solution:

Express \(F_y\) in terms of \(F\): \(F_y = F\cos\beta = F\cos 75^\circ\).
Substitute into the magnitude relation \(F^2 = F_x^2 + F_y^2 + F_z^2\): \[F^2 = (1.5)^2 + (F\cos 75^\circ)^2 + (1.25)^2 \implies F^2(1 - \cos^2 75^\circ) = 3.8125\] \[F = \frac{\sqrt{3.8125}}{\sin 75^\circ} = 2.02\text{ kN}\] \[F_y = 2.021\cos 75^\circ = 0.523\text{ kN}\]
